findings.quote: Adding or removing a pure solid or pure liquid does not shift the equilibrium, because it is not in $K$.
findings.problem: This general statement, added in the round-1 fix, fails for a known exception: adding water, a pure liquid, to an aqueous equilibrium does shift it. The added water dilutes every dissolved species. When the two sides have different numbers of dissolved particles, Q moves away from K and the system shifts toward the side with more dissolved particles. Example: CoCl4(2-)(aq) + 6H2O(l) = Co(H2O)6(2+)(aq) + 4Cl-(aq) has water in the equation and left out of K, yet adding water turns the blue solution pink (a shift to the right, 1 dissolved particle on the left and 5 on the right). A student who follows the sentence answers 'no shift'. The lesson's other rules do not cover this case: it has a volume rule for gases but no dilution rule for solutions. So this differs from the round-1 pressure finding that the lead downgraded. Heterogeneous cases such as adding CaCO3(s) to CaCO3(s) = CaO(s) + CO2(g) stay correct.
findings.source: Q versus K reasoning, OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 13.2 Equilibrium Constants and 13.3 Shifting Equilibria; RSC Education experiment 'The equilibrium between two coloured cobalt species' (adding water reverses the chloride shift; seen through a search summary, the page refused a direct fetch); checklist B01; reader-rules 'Added after the Sol audit'

findings.quote: The orders are found by experiment.
findings.problem: This sentence is in a paragraph of five sentences (from 'The square brackets mean' to 'the steps of the reaction'). Other paragraphs also have more than three: the spontaneity paragraph ('A reaction is spontaneous when' to 'the temperature decides', five), the K paragraph ('Products are on top' to 'how fast equilibrium is reached', five), and the rate paragraph, the fair-test paragraph and both equilibrium paragraphs (four each). The guide allows one to three short sentences per paragraph.
